stem: A straight-line supply curve through the origin has a PES of exactly 1 at every point.
explanation: True. Quantity changes in the same proportion as price along such a line.

stem: A rise in the price of a good shifts the supply curve to the right.
explanation: False. A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the supply curve; PES measures that movement.

stem: Name the type of supply curve that is horizontal.
explanation: A horizontal supply curve shows firms will supply any quantity at one price: perfectly elastic.

stem: Define price elasticity of supply.

points.description: A measure of the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price.
% change in quantity supplied divided by % change in price.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Price elasticity of supply measures how responsive the quantity supplied of a good is to a change in its own price. It is the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.

explanation: Responsiveness and formula.

stem: Explain **two** factors that determine the price elasticity of supply of a good.

points.description: Factor 1 identified (for example spare capacity or stocks).
Factor 1 explained: spare capacity lets output rise quickly, so supply is more elastic.
Factor 2 identified (for example time period, factor mobility or perishability).
Factor 2 explained: for example a longer time lets firms adjust all factors, so supply is more elastic.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Spare capacity: if firms have idle machines or workers, they can raise output quickly when price rises, so supply is elastic. Time period: the longer the time allowed, the more factors firms can change and the more new firms can enter, so supply becomes more elastic.

explanation: Two determinants, each explained.
hints: Name the factor and say whether it makes supply more or less elastic.

stem: Analyse why the price of fresh vegetables often changes sharply when demand changes.

points.description: Supply of fresh vegetables is inelastic in the short run.
Crops take time to grow and perishables cannot be stored for long.
A change in demand therefore cannot be met by a large change in quantity.
Price has to change by a large amount to restore equilibrium.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Fresh vegetables take time to grow and cannot be stored for long, so supply is inelastic in the short run. When demand rises, quantity supplied cannot increase much, so the price has to rise by a large amount to ration the available supply; similarly a fall in demand causes a large fall in price.

explanation: Inelastic supply leads to larger price changes.

parts.label: (a)

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain **two** reasons why supply is more elastic after three years.

points.description: Farmers can plant more land and buy equipment (all factors can change).

stem: Assess why the prices of agricultural products tend to fluctuate more than the prices of manufactured goods.

points.description: Agricultural supply is inelastic in the short run: growing time, weather, perishability.
Manufacturing can use spare capacity and stocks to respond to price.
Demand for food is inelastic, so shifts in supply cause large price changes.
Harvests vary with weather and pests, so supply shifts often.
Storage, imports and buffer stocks can reduce fluctuations.
Some manufactured goods also have volatile prices (commodity-based inputs).
Long-run supply is more elastic.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, applied and developed, with a justified conclusion.
Some development of one or both sides, limited application or conclusion.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Agricultural supply is inelastic in the short run because crops take time to grow and perishable produce cannot be stored, and harvests vary with the weather, so supply shifts frequently. Demand for food is also inelastic, so any shift in supply produces a large change in price. Manufacturers can use spare capacity and stocks to adjust output quickly, which stabilises prices. However, storage, imports and buffer stock schemes can reduce agricultural fluctuations, and some manufactured goods depend on volatile raw material prices. In the long run supply becomes more elastic. Overall, the combination of inelastic supply, inelastic demand and weather-driven shifts explains the greater volatility of farm prices.

explanation: Contrast supply and demand elasticities in the two sectors and weigh offsetting factors.
